steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Known attacks" section for a Wikipedia article on acoustic cryptanalysis, summarizing the main published attacks that recover keystrokes, keys or printed data from sound.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Keyboard and keypad acoustic attacks
- Acoustic timing attacks on CPUs and RSA key extraction
- Why coils and capacitors emit sound
- Printer attacks
- Speaker/headphone and screen attacks; later key extraction work

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Keyboard and keypad attacks
  - 2004: Dmitri Asonov and Rakesh Agrawal, IBM Almaden Research Center
  - computer keyboards, telephone keypads, ATMs vulnerable via key sounds
  - neural network recognizes key pressed; recorded sounds -> recover entered text
  - covert listening devices -> passwords, passphrases, PINs, other input
  - 2005: UC Berkeley group, practical experiments confirming threat
- CPU timing attacks
  - also 2004: Adi Shamir and Eran Tromer; timing attacks on CPU doing crypto via acoustic emission variations
  - ultrasonic noise from capacitors and inductors on motherboards; not EM emissions, not audible fan hum
  - later with Daniel Genkin and others: attack on laptop running GnuPG (RSA implementation)
  - mobile phone close to laptop, or lab-grade microphone up to 4 m away
  - results published December 2013
- Physical cause
  - small movements in coils and capacitors when current surge passes
  - capacitors change diameter: electrostatic attraction/repulsion or piezoelectric size change in layers
  - conversely microphonic; high-end audio industry reduces microphonics (immissions) in coils and capacitors; they muddy hi-fi amplifier sound
- Printers
  - March 2015: inkjet printers with ultrasonic heads read back with high frequency MEMS microphones; unique signal per nozzle; timing reconstruction with known printed data ("confidential" in 12-point font)
  - thermal printers: similar, less fidelity, weaker bursting-bubble signals
  - hack: microphone, chip storage IC, burst transmitter, long-life Li+ battery in doctored cartridges sent by post to target (typically a bank); retrieved from garbage using challenge-response RFID chip
  - dot-matrix printer printout reconstruction publicized 2011
- Speakers/screens and later work
  - Ben-Gurion University Cybersecurity Research Center (Israel): data extracted using computer speakers and headphones
  - Forbes report: seeing displayed information via microphone, 96.5% accuracy
  - 2016: Genkin, Shamir, Tromer paper; key extraction from laptop acoustic emissions during decryption; simple mobile phone and more sensitive microphone

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In 2004 Dmitri Asonov and Rakesh Agrawal from the IBM Almaden Research Center announced that computer keyboards, and keypads on telephones and automated teller machines (ATMs), are vulnerable to attacks that are based on the sounds that different keys make. Their attack used a neural network to recognize which key was pressed. They analyzed recorded sounds and were able to recover the text of the data that was entered. With these techniques an attacker who uses covert listening devices can get passwords, passphrases, personal identification numbers (PINs), and other information that is entered with keyboards. In 2005 a group of researchers at UC Berkeley did a number of practical experiments that showed this kind of threat is valid.

Also in 2004, Adi Shamir and Eran Tromer showed that it may be possible to do timing attacks against a CPU that is performing cryptographic operations, by analyzing variations in acoustic emissions. The emissions they analyzed were ultrasonic noise coming from capacitors and inductors on computer motherboards. They were not electromagnetic emissions and not the humming of a cooling fan that humans can hear. Shamir and Tromer then worked with a new collaborator, Daniel Genkin, and others, and they successfully implemented the attack on a laptop running a version of GnuPG (an RSA implementation). They used either a mobile phone that was close to the laptop or a laboratory-grade microphone up to 4 m away. They published their experimental results in December 2013.

Coils and capacitors make acoustic emissions because of small movements when a current surge goes through them. Capacitors especially change their diameter slightly as their many layers experience electrostatic attraction/repulsion or piezoelectric size change. A coil or capacitor that emits acoustic noise will also be microphonic, the other way round, and the high-end audio industry takes steps with coils and capacitors to reduce these microphonics (immissions), because they can muddy the sound of a hi-fi amplifier.

- Printers
  - March 2015: inkjet printers with ultrasonic heads read back with high frequency MEMS microphones; unique signal per nozzle; timing reconstruction with known printed data ("confidential" in 12-point font)
  - thermal printers: similar, less fidelity, weaker bursting-bubble signals
  - hack: microphone, chip storage IC, burst transmitter, long-life Li+ battery in doctored cartridges sent by post to target (typically a bank); retrieved from garbage using challenge-response RFID chip
  - dot-matrix printer printout reconstruction publicized 2011
- Speakers/screens and later work
  - Ben-Gurion University Cybersecurity Research Center (Israel): data extracted using computer speakers and headphones
  - Forbes report: seeing displayed information via microphone, 96.5% accuracy
  - 2016: Genkin, Shamir, Tromer paper; key extraction from laptop acoustic emissions during decryption; simple mobile phone and more sensitive microphone

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In 2004 Dmitri Asonov and Rakesh Agrawal from the IBM Almaden Research Center announced that computer keyboards, and keypads on telephones and automated teller machines (ATMs), are vulnerable to attacks that are based on the sounds that different keys make. Their attack used a neural network to recognize which key was pressed. They analyzed recorded sounds and were able to recover the text of the data that was entered. With these techniques an attacker who uses covert listening devices can get passwords, passphrases, personal identification numbers (PINs), and other information that is entered with keyboards. In 2005 a group of researchers at UC Berkeley did a number of practical experiments that showed this kind of threat is valid.

Also in 2004, Adi Shamir and Eran Tromer showed that it may be possible to do timing attacks against a CPU that is performing cryptographic operations, by analyzing variations in acoustic emissions. The emissions they analyzed were ultrasonic noise coming from capacitors and inductors on computer motherboards. They were not electromagnetic emissions and not the humming of a cooling fan that humans can hear. Shamir and Tromer then worked with a new collaborator, Daniel Genkin, and others, and they successfully implemented the attack on a laptop running a version of GnuPG (an RSA implementation). They used either a mobile phone that was close to the laptop or a laboratory-grade microphone up to 4 m away. They published their experimental results in December 2013.

Coils and capacitors make acoustic emissions because of small movements when a current surge goes through them. Capacitors especially change their diameter slightly as their many layers experience electrostatic attraction/repulsion or piezoelectric size change. A coil or capacitor that emits acoustic noise will also be microphonic, the other way round, and the high-end audio industry takes steps with coils and capacitors to reduce these microphonics (immissions), because they can muddy the sound of a hi-fi amplifier.

In March 2015 it was made public that some inkjet printers that use ultrasonic heads can be read back. This is done by using high frequency MEMS microphones to record the unique acoustic signals from each nozzle and using timing reconstruction with known printed data, that is, "confidential" in 12-point font. Thermal printers can also be read with similar methods, but with less fidelity because the signals from the bursting bubbles are weaker. The hack also involved putting a microphone, chip storage IC and burst transmitter with a long-life Li+ battery into doctored cartridges. These were substituted for genuine ones sent by post to the target, which was typically a bank, and then retrieved from the garbage using a challenge-response RFID chip. Similar work on reconstructing printouts from dot-matrix printers was publicized in 2011.

A research team at the Cybersecurity Research Center of Ben-Gurion University in Israel discovered a new acoustic cryptanalysis technique that lets data be extracted using the speakers and headphones of a computer. Forbes published a report saying that researchers found a way to see information being displayed by using a microphone, with 96.5% accuracy.

In 2016 Genkin, Shamir, and Tromer published another paper describing a key extraction attack that relied on the acoustic emissions from laptop devices during decryption. They showed that the attack worked with both a simple mobile phone and a more sensitive microphone.
